knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\cot{\left(u \right)},\qquad u=\cos{\left(x - 8 \right)}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=- \cot^{2}{\left(u \right)} - 1,\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \sin{\left(x - 8 \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ &=- \cot^{2}{\left(u \right)} - 1\cdot (- \sin{\left(x - 8 \right)}) \\ &=- \left(- \cot^{2}{\left(\cos{\left(x - 8 \right)} \right)} - 1\right) \sin{\left(x - 8 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{cos}\left(x-8\right).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}\left(x-8\right).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\left(x-8\right)) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}\left(x-8\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}\left(x-8\right)).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =2 \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}$ at the point $\left(3,\sqrt{3} \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 3$ is given by $f'(3).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = 2 \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} - \frac{\pi}{6}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - 2 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x - 3 \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- 2 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x - 3 \right)})\\
&=- 2 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \cos{\left(x - 3 \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=3,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(3)&=- 2 \sin{\left(- \frac{\pi}{6} + \sin{\left(0 \right)} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-2 \cdot - \frac{1}{2} \\
        &=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(3,\sqrt{3}) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(\sqrt{3}\right) &= (1)\cdot\left(x-(3)\right)\\
y&=x - 3 + \sqrt{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =6 \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)}$ at the point $\left(3,- 3 \sqrt{2} \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 3$ is given by $f'(3).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = 6 \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - 6 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x - 3 \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x - 3 \right)})\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x - 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(x - 3 \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=3,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(3)&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(0 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-6 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\
        &=- 3 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(3,- 3 \sqrt{2}) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(- 3 \sqrt{2}\right) &= (- 3 \sqrt{2})\cdot\left(x-(3)\right)\\
y&=- 3 \sqrt{2} x + 6 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =6 \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)}$ at the point $\left(0,- 3 \sqrt{2} \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = 6 \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - 6 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)})\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(0)&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(0 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-6 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\
        &=- 3 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,- 3 \sqrt{2}) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(- 3 \sqrt{2}\right) &= (- 3 \sqrt{2})\cdot\left(x-(0)\right)\\
y&=- 3 \sqrt{2} x - 3 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =6 \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x + 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)}$ at the point $\left(-3,- 3 \sqrt{2} \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = -3$ is given by $f'(-3).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = 6 \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x + 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - 6 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x + 3 \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x + 3 \right)})\\
&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x + 3 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(x + 3 \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=-3,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(-3)&=- 6 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(0 \right)} + \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-6 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\
        &=- 3 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(-3,- 3 \sqrt{2}) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(- 3 \sqrt{2}\right) &= (- 3 \sqrt{2})\cdot\left(x-(-3)\right)\\
y&=- 3 \sqrt{2} x - 12 \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = \csc{u}, \qquad u = \cos\left(x-8\right).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -\csc{u}\cot u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin\left(x-8\right).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=-\csc u \cot u \cdot  (-\sin\left(x-8\right))\\

&=\sin\left(x-8\right)\csc \left(\cos\left(x-8\right)\right) \cot \left(\cos\left(x-8\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{sin}\left(x-1\right).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}\left(x-1\right).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}\left(x-1\right) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}\left(x-1\right)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}\left(x-1\right)).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=2\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{sin}\left(x+8\right).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=2\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}\left(x+8\right).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}\left(x+8\right) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}\left(x+8\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{sin}\left(x+8\right))\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{sin}\left(x+8\right)).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=3\operatorname{sec}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{cos}\left(x-7\right).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=3\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}\left(x-7\right).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\left(x-7\right)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}\left(x-7\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{cos}\left(x-7\right))\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{cos}\left(x-7\right)).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=2 \sin{\left(u \right)},\qquad u=\sin{\left(x + 5 \right)}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=2 \cos{\left(u \right)},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\cos{\left(x + 5 \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ &=2 \cos{\left(u \right)}\cdot (\cos{\left(x + 5 \right)}) \\ &=2 \cos{\left(x + 5 \right)} \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x + 5 \right)} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$
